div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: —Outside of County Gaol—Houses and Trees representing the Street in a Country Town— a Bridge in the Centre, and extensive open Country behind it—Stage partly darken'd—Lauretta St Orme seen crossing the Bridge with a Basket in her Hand.

sp.p: Hark!
it was the sound of feet!—I'm watch'd—I am discover'd! —
Oh Heavens!— my rash imprudent zeal has ruin'd all—no—

'twas but fancy—nothing but the passing breeze!—and I may venture to proceed.—I know —I'm sure that he'll condemn me; but 'tis a long, long month since I have heard what passes in that dark abode—perhaps his health may suffer by confinement —perhaps his poverty denies him e'en life's common comforts—perhaps—Oh! the suspense is insupportable! and I were not the daughter that he thinks me, if I endur'd it calmly—
—I will but ask, and then again to my retreat.

sp.speaker: Gaoler
sp.p: Who's there at this time of the morning?

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: One to enquire after Mr. St. Orme.

sp.speaker: Gaoler.
sp.p: St. Orme!—the prisoner confin'd for murder?

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Ay: as 'tis said, for murder!

sp.speaker: Gaoler.
sp.p: You can't see him—begone.

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Stay sir—spare me but a moment— I will not ask to see him—I only ask that you will give him this.
sp.stage: (Taking a small paper parcel out of basket.)
sp.p: —'tis a small present from a stranger— meant to revive and cheer him—nay:—if he be guilty, he the more needs consolation—the virtuous fly to conscience for relief—but where!—Oh! where, can such as you describe St. Orme, seek comfort or repose?—then be merciful—and in the hour of distress, you shall have your reward.

sp.speaker: Gaoler.
sp.p: Well—I'll take it.
sp.stage: (Opens grating—takes parcel—shuts it again and exit.)

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Thanks—thanks!—and yet those prison gates—Oh! that they'd open wide, and once more give a father to my arms!—then should my humble talents still assist him—then would we seek again that hapless mother, who needs a husband's and a daughter's aid.—But these are idle hopes—the dreaded hour approaches!—the day of trial is at hand!—Oh spare him!—spare him Heaven!

sp.speaker: Gaoler.
sp.p: So—instead of reviving the prisoner, your present threw him into violent agitation—and here—
—he sends you this answer.

sp.speaker: Lauretta
sp.p: “You have done very wrong—return instantly to your retreat in the mountains; and never forget that you alone were present at the murder—that there's no other witness to convict me; 'tis for your sake and your unfortunate mother's that I wish to live—Conceal yourself but four days longer, and we may still meet and still be happy!”— Oh! let me fly to my retreat!—Tell him I cheerfully obey his wishes, and thank him for his counsel.
sp.stage: (Gaoler exit, and Lauretta going up stage, stops on seeing it lit.)
sp.p: —Ha! the morning breaks, and the broad glare of day will lead to my discovery!—unseen, to reach the mountains is impossible! —weak, thoughtless girl!—to risk so much for selfish—momentary joy!—What's to be done?—I know—hard by, there is a thick impervious wood—there, I'll secrete myself till night, and then set forth again—and if thy safety rests on my concealment, fear not my father!—we will be happy still.

div.stage: Enter Sternly and two Servants of Sir Edward Delauny's.

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Come—bustle—to your daily occupation lads—search every where for the witness, and recollect how near 'tis to the assizes.

sp.speaker: 1st Servant.
sp.p: We do—But when you recollect 'tis now five months since Sir Frederick's death, and that we've hunted for this Miss Lauretta every day—

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Ay: plague on her: she got all this knowledge of tricks, shifts, and disguises, from turning stage player—but the present baronet is bent upon revenge, and that the trial may be properly conducted, he expects this very morning a great London Solicitor—one Mr. Postpone—fam'd for integrity and talent—and if our only evidence be not forthcoming, how can even he assist us!— so away—lose not a moment, whilst I wait his arrival at the inn.
—Yes: yes: I must look about me like Sir Edward, for if Mr. St. Orme don't suffer, I fancy somebody else will.

sp.speaker: Henry Sapling
sp.p: There!—there, you rogues!

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Hah!—Who comes here?—Surely not the London lawyer already.
No—as I live, Mr. Henry Sapling! who has been at sea these four years—the nephew of my old neighbour. —I wonder whether he's the same unsuspicious, simple youth he us'd to be.

div.stage: Enter Henry Sapling in a naval uniform, follow'd by two Post-boys.

sp.speaker: Henry
sp.p: There—that's for the chaise and four—and here—here's a guinea for yourselves
—What, Sternly! —my old acquaintance Sternly!—why, how you stare and gape.—I dare say, now, you think this extravagant travelling.

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: To be sure I do.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Well—it's very likely—but I'm just come from sea, to touch a legacy; and, between ourselves—we sailors are so unus'd to accounts and economy and—in short, I feel money such a load to me, that I see I shan't sail pleasantly till I've chuck'd it all overboard.—But, I say—how's nunky?

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Oh—quite a new man since you saw him.—Why 'tis but a fortnight ago, he married Sir Edward's cousin.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Married is he?—Thank Fortune!—So am not I, Master Steward.

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Why thank Fortune?—I think I could recommend a wife to you, Mr. Sapling.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Whose wife?—Not nunky's, I hope.

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: No—his ward—the lovely Miss Honoria, who was brought up with you.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Psha—don't talk of it—she's a charming creature!—but a wife!—do you know, Sternly, in all the storms and battles I've encounter'd, that was my consolation—says I—“never mind—blow on, my boys!—you're nothing to the gales of matrimony.” —No—give me quiet—independence— liberty—give me Lady Sensitive.

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Lady Sensitive!—Who's Lady Sensitive?

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Mum—say nothing—met her at the Opera—pick'd up her fan—handed her to her low chariot—receiv'd her card—call'd next morning— neat house in Mary-le-bone—green blinds— flower-pots—singing birds—black boys—white liveries—and she and her maid so fashionably dress'd, that, upon my honour, all their clothes put together only weigh'd two ounces, three scruples.

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Psha—this is a trick—she'll lead you into dissipation.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: No—she'll make me domestic—she's so fond of me, that if perchance I dine at the coffee-house, she sends me twenty messages before the cloth's remov'd—and if I don't return at the moment she expects me—poor soul! she goes into a fit!—yes, she does—I find her screaming, and the whole house swimming with hartshorn, laudanum, and cordials—there's tenderness!—there's love for you!

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Love with a vengeance!—but pray— about the load?—
. Don't she help you chuck some of it overboard?

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: No—there's the worst of her—she's so proud, and so disinterested, that, except now and then allowing me to pay her coachmaker, and her upholsterer, and her milliner.—Oh, yes;—she carries it so far, that t'other day, when her humanity threw her into a spunging house, she didn't let me know it, for a whole half hour, Sternly!—But I forget—I promised to return in three days, and every post overset the mail with love letters.—And that I may be punctual, now to visit nunky.—

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Stop—that isn't the way—to divert Sir Edward's gloom, he and Mrs. Sapling keep the honeymoon at Delauny house—and there you'll find Miss Honoria also—and so, good day—

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Pooh! What do I care for Miss Honoria? I tell you the word “Wife” is to me slavery —chains—leaks—short allowance—sea-sickness —and a press-gang—no—let me be a free man —go where I like—do what I like—stay— Zounds! there's the mail coach—I must make haste with my love-letters, or there'll be more fits, hartshorn, laudanum, and cordials.

div.head: Scene

sp.speaker: Paul Postpone
sp.p: Waiter! Waiter!

sp.speaker: Waiter
sp.p: Coming, sir—coming.

sp.speaker: Paul
sp.p: Where is this room, and the wine, and the sandwiches?

sp.speaker: Waiter
sp.p: Here, your honour—all ready.

div.stage: Enter Paul Postpone in a Travelling Dress—his Clerk with a Bag—and two Waiters, with Table, Chairs, Wine, and Sandwiches.

sp.speaker: Paul
sp.stage: (taking off his Hat, and puffing and fanning himself).
sp.p: Pheugh!—What a fagging life is mine!—Never a moment's relaxation!—No sooner the drudgery of term over, than brought from London to slave of the Assizes here—and on a Saturday—the day I always run down to my Brentford villa—but here
—here's consolation—Clerk! sit down, Clerk.

sp.speaker: Clerk.
sp.p: Sir, I thank you—but really it is time to go into the case now—consider, sir, you have so put it off from day to day, that you hav'n't even read your client's instructions.

sp.speaker: Paul
sp.p: —Psha—time enough to-morrow—and never—never talk business on an empty stomach,
—Waiter! —tell us something about your town—whose fine seat is that on the hill?

sp.speaker: Waiter.
sp.p: Mr. Scrip's—a stock-jobber, sir.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: And the large stone house in the valley?

sp.speaker: Waiter.
sp.p: Mr. Shortstuff's, sir—another stock-jobber.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Two stock-jobbers!—damme, that's too much for one town.—Clerk, here's, “may lame ducks multiply.”

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Mr. Postpone, I understand—happy to wait on a gentleman so celebrated for honesty— industry—

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Sir!
sp.stage: (bowing in return, but not quitting his seat.)

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: I am sent by Sir Edward Delauny, to beg you'll come instantly to his house, and consult on the case.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Sir, my compliments to Sir Edward,— and, in the first place, never stir till the bottle's out —and, in the next, bid him not be afraid—I'll bring him off.

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Bring him off!—why, he's the prosecutor.

sp.speaker: Clerk
sp.p: —There, sir, I told you how it would be.

sp.speaker: Paul
sp.p: True—true—as you say, he's the prosecutor—and the prisoner's name is Thomson —no—Johnstone—no—but stop—stop— what was I going to ask you?—something very material—oh—does Sir Edward keep hounds?

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: And hunters?

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: And pray—any steel traps in the neighbourhood? —for once at my Brentford villa, my horse was caught by the foreleg, and smash went I —right through a cucumber frame.—Laid me up a whole term—

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Sir, I'm very sorry; but with submission, we are all most anxious for your opinion; and if our only witness can't be found, what think you of that part of the case, about the Scotch marriage? —of a poor half-pay lieutenant, like St. Orme, deluding thus the noble Miss Delauny?

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Scotch—Oh, ay:—I recollect now— but that won't do—will it, Clerk?—no—there's no legal harm in Scotch marriages; because if the parties chuse to stay there nine months, the first child is a Northcountryman; and, to their credit, they always provide for their families.—That's my opinion—and now, let the rest stand over—enough —quite enough for one morning.

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Nay: Sir Edward is waiting, and Mr. and Mrs. Sapling expect you at their Sylvan fête.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Sylvan fête!

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Aye: an entertainment of dancing and singing, given to amuse their host, and celebrate their wedding.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Come along, Clerk—now the morning's broke in upon, we may as well make a day of it; and in a few years—Yes: let me work in the hard manner I do now, only a few years longer, and I'll give musical parties!—Though a dealer in discord, I delight in harmony, and, if singing be a requisite—I'll chaunt a bill of costs with any gentleman on the roll.

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Stay, sir.—One word in private—Sir Edward bid me hint to you, that in case of conviction, your fees should be trebled.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Then Sir Edward did wrong.—If the poor fellow's guilty, let him suffer—if not, bribes shan't convict him; law is sufficiently profitable, without a man turning rascal to live by it.—Yes, sir: and, much as I like business, I've no objection to a little pleasure, and how can I feel any if I submit to be corrupted.—Come, Clerk—to-morrow for labour —to-day for mirth and revelry.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE.—Delauny House at a distance—Park Gates opening to extensive Park.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Away to town express—say that I feel her absence insupportable, and will return to-night —yet stop—what's this you tell me about poor St. Orme?

sp.speaker: Thomas.
sp.p: Why, sir—I heard that Lieutenant St. Orme, who sail'd home with us from America, was now in the county gaol.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Impossible!—but if it prove as you relate, he and his daughter shall not want a friend—no— I will seek Lauretta and her father—

sp.speaker: Thomas.
sp.p: Seek his daughter!—Lord, sir—you quite frighten me—you forget that Lady Sensitive is so anxious to keep you to herself, sir—

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: So she is—'tis a pleasure to think of it— sweet susceptible soul!—don't you remember the day before we left town, Tom, how she burst into tears when I patted her lap-dog?—“I see,”—said she—“your partiality, and either I or that little ugly French monster leave the house, Mr. Sapling!” —and afterwards at dinner, when I prais'd the dressing of some of the made dishes—“I was right,”—said she—and she rush'd down stairs, and discharged the cook instantly.—Oh! these are all proofs of her affection and my happiness—so mind —not a word of St. Orme and Lauretta.
. —And now to visit nunky at Delauny house here—

.—Ha!— Who is that young lady walking and reading in the park?—upon my word, something very handsome and very extraordinary!—I don't think I ever saw any thing of this kind in London—she's certainly very different from Lady Sensitive, and yet —somehow not at all uninteresting!—she's coming this way—'gad! if I thought Tom were out of sight, and her ladyship wouldn't hear of it. I should like just to ascertain—she's here!—So it's no fault of mine—every body sees I can't help myself.

div.stage: Enter Honoria through the Park Gate with a Book.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Welcome to England, sir—after an absence of four tedious years, welcome to your native home.

sp.speaker: Henry
sp.p: Madam!—I—I—

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: What! don't you recollect me?— Nay: that's unkind, Mr. Henry—forget the companion of your early years!—forget Honoria!

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Honoria!—bless my soul—how you are improv'd!—that is, alter'd—that is—I mean how different you are from the London ladies.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: What!—because you find me reading? —Nay: you wrong them—

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: I don't—they never open a book—never —for I know one, a most accomplish'd lady, who reads nothing but the play-bills—and then again, you look so mild—so contented—so healthy.— I dare say now, you have no fits.

sp.speaker: Honoria
sp.p: Fits!—Never.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: What a blessing!—But if you had a lover, and that lover patted your lap-dog, I hope you'd turn the little ugly French monster out of the house, Honoria.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Do you?—Now I should like the little animal the better, and more caress it, since my lover prais'd it.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: 'Gad!—that never struck me—and you are such a charming—fascinating—

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: —“What's life without passion! —sweet passion of love?”

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: 'Sdeath! what love-sick blockhead's this, to interrupt us?

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Why! don't you know your own uncle?

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: That!—that foppish, capering little fellow my uncle!

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Yes:—the simple country 'squire is converted into a modern fine gentleman, and, instead of farming and hunting, he devotes his whole time to fashion and frivolity.—Such is the influence of his town-bred wife!

div.stage: Enter Sapling, foppishly dress'd, humming tune, strutting, &c.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Ah, Henry!—How are you, Henry?

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Sir, I give you joy—not only of marrying a baronet's cousin,—but of your improv'd style of dress and address, Sir!

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Why, yes: I've got on—thanks to my darling wife and her fashionable lessons—you perceive —I'm almost finish'd.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Almost!—it strikes me you are quite finish'd?

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: No—there's still room for improvement —for last night at Lady Squeeze's route, I shew'd the most barbarous ignorance—my wife told me if I play'd at cards, I must pay for them —very well!—so far I did right—I pop'd down my half crown for card-money—but, as luck would have it, a man came round with cakes and lemonade, and, thinks I, if Lady Squeeze can't afford to pay for one thing, of course she can't for another, and so, Ecod!—I pop'd down half a crown for them also.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: And I should have done the same—they can get nothing by cakes and lemonade—but I thought they got enough by cards without charging their friends for them.—Well!—and the farm-house, Honoria? Is the old farm-house as much beautified as its owner?

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Quite.—Isn't it, guardian?

sp.speaker: Sapling
sp.p: Yes:—the barn is turn'd into a ball-room—the pigeon-house over it into a billiard-room—the calf-house near it, into a concert-room—and the house for cows and horn'd cattle, into a state bed-room for me and Mrs. Sapling. Then the parlour is so enlarg'd—do you know, it will now sup a hundred enemies?

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Enemies!—You mean friends.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: No—I don't—I mean enemies—to be sure I thought as you did, and so I told Mrs. Sapling. —Says I, “Now's the time, my life, to be reveng'd on your enemies—mortify them, by not asking them.”—“No,” says she, “I'll mortify them by asking them!—the delight of visiting people is to vex each other, and my superior rooms will goad them to the soul!—Oh, yes:— and for friends, Mr. Sapling—never enlarge your parlour on their account—a closet will at any time hold them!”—But with all this, marriage has one inconvenience—
. —I've been obliged to give up hunting, Henry.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Give up hunting, sir!

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Yes:—Mrs. Sapling's late husband stupidly broke his neck by it; and now, if I were to ride and risk mine—poor soul!—you can easily enter into her feelings, Henry.

sp.speaker: Henry
sp.p: I can, sir:— Your estate is in annuity, and if you fall, the whole falls with you.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: No, sir—that's not her motive—'tis pure unbounded love, sir—and therefore I've conceal'd my passion for horses, and parted with them all—all but my favourite hunter Arabella—I keep her privately from gratitude—but hush!—here's my wife's friend Mr. Privilege!—not a word of it to him, for they tell one another every thing.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Indeed!—and you not jealous?

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Jealous!—that's very well—look who you're talking to; and know, that handsome people are never jealous—besides it's out—it is'n't in fashion!

div.stage: Enter Privilege through the Park Gates.

sp.speaker: Privilege.
sp.p: Oh, my dear sir—you'll be so fascinated —our charming Mrs. Sapling has composed such a grand duet for to-night's fête—and I'm to sing the principal part, and you and Miss Honoria are to come and hear it rehears'd.—

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: And you also, Henry—and to oblige you as a stranger, she shall play all her other musical compositions—her first part of the essay on man—half Clarissa Harlowe—and the whole of two German oratorios.

sp.speaker: Privilege.
sp.p: Aye: and all my love verses to Honoria; —who, by the bye, Sapling, I've at last made up my mind to marry.—I have, upon my soul, Ma'am—this morning I got my own consent, and as to asking yours, or any body's else, that's quite unnecessary—because, you know, I'm a privileg'd man.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: A privileg'd man, sir!

sp.speaker: Privilege.
sp.p: Yes, sir: if you or any common jogtrot person were to propose in this manner,—or make love to married ladies, and run away with them—or borrow money, and not pay it—you'd stand a good chance of being scouted, kick'd, and hang'd for it:—but if I do these things, every body laughs and exclaims—“don't mind him—he's a privileg'd man!”—now, sir, do you comprehend?

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: I do, sir—every body laughs at you, and nobody minds you—I hope, uncle, that's your opinion; —but unluckily, I can't stay to hear that, or the music now—no—first let me visit poor St. Orme.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: St. Orme!—you know him then?

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Intimately.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: I knew his wife, and therefore feel for him.—If that is your engagement, we must spare you; but soon return—you see, I need your friendship also.

sp.speaker: Privilege.
sp.p: Very likely: but I wouldn't advise the gentleman to think of marrying you, or indeed any body—because now-a-days wives are such expensive articles, that none can afford them but privileg'd men. But come, Sapling, we forget the duet, and your wife will be quite jealous at my staying.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Jealous at your—! Oh! it's all right—I'm not suspicious—no—so fond a partner and so true a friend, may play duets as often as they please. You see, Mr. Annuity!
— this is Honoria's husband!

div.stage: [Exeunt—Honoria between Sapling and Privilege, and looking back at Henry —Privilege strutting and smiling contemptuously on Henry.

sp.speaker: Henry
sp.p: 'Sdeath! can she endure one moment such a flutterer? If she does, I'll chop him into messes. I'll—but hold—hold— where's her ladyship all this time?—the tender, the accomplish'd—Zounds! I wonder whether there ever was such a thing as a man loving two women at the same time?—I'm afraid not. And if there was, could any man ever manage two women at the same time?—there's certainly no living instance—so, farewell Honoria—farewell, thou dear bewitching—. Oh, damme—what signifies talking here—she can't hear me at this distance— so every body sees going after her is no fault of mine again.

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: I cannot rest. Now as the awful hour approaches, my fears accumulate beyond endurance. Life I could yield up manfully; but to part with those, that once—and still might render life a blessing—my wife!—my child!—shall I ne'er more behold them!

sp.speaker: Henry Sapling
sp.p: Where is he?—Where is Lieutenant St. Orme?

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: Ha! Who's here?

sp.speaker: Gaoler
sp.p: This way, sir.

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: 'Tis Henry, 'tis my friend!

sp.speaker: Gaoler.
sp.p: There sir—there is the prisoner.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Charles!
sp.stage: (takes his hand and bursts into tears.)
sp.p: —Damnation!—I meant to behave like a man, but the word “prisoner”—come back you rascal, and I'll teach you to make a British sailor expose himself.

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: Nay: your tears become you Henry; and if now they fall, what will they do when in a few short days—

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Don't—if you are guilty, don't utter it. I won't hear it—won't bear it—never will believe that Charles St. Orme—that my friend, would seek the life of any man.

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: Then you're deceiv'd—I sought Sir Frederick's life, and by this arm he fell!

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Indeed!

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: Hear—hear my vindication!—'Tis now near eighteen years since my Amelia chose me for her husband; and for this high offence, she was deserted by her father—the rash, yet wrong'd Sir Frederick. We left the country—fled to America —and, by the sale of my commission, purchased an humble farm; which till a year ago supplied our moderate wants.—Then illness drove me from my avocation; and though Lauretta labour'd for our aid, distress so rapidly pursued us, that my fond wife—still clinging to the wretch her family despised —set forth for England; and not ten months past, arriv'd alone, a beggar at that gate, that but for me had ne'er been shut against her.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Well: go on.—On seeing her, did her father persist?

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: Oh, yes: with unabating rancour—he never could forgive my poverty and birth. And now observe, and shudder as you hear it!—In a few weeks he wrote me to America, that his wrong'd daughter had detected my intrigues—knew I had sent her home, to carry on a low clandestine love—and maddening at my falsehood and deceit, was fever'd to delirium—was insane! I answer'd hastily I knew not what, and flew to her assistance. I arriv'd—I ask'd for her abode—when—death and shame!—he said the care of her was his alone, and that a perjur'd husband should not see her!

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Not see her!

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: No; his aim was separation: and to secure it, he defam'd me first—then robb'd me of the power to justify myself, and solace her.—What could I do?—I knew the law would give me ample justice; but burning with impatience and revenge, was I to wait a form so tedious?—No—I rush'd into his presence—my daughter follow'd to detain me—I persisted in my resolution, and demanded satisfaction—this he declin'd—I presented him a pistol—he grasp'd it to defend his life—which I conceiving an acceptance of my challenge, and wild with fury and with wrongs, fir'd!—he fell; and in a few short months—Oh my friend! I see you tremble at my rashness; he was Amelia's father, and I deserve a death more terrible than his!

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: No; I tremble from another cause—the proof:—who can give proof against you?

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: None, but my daughter; and she is purposely concealed: if she remain so till the trial's past, I'm free to trace and rescue her I love; but if she's found, I fall—and she, poor girl—her mother robb'd of reason, and her father by her own evidence!—Oh! I can bear all but this.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: And so can I: therefore good b'w'ye.

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: Why—where are you going?

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: To Sir Edward—to your new antagonist; and I'll ask him civilly—very civilly—not to search after Lauretta;—but if that won't do, and he persists in forcing a daughter to convict her own father—talk of pistols, my dear fellow—I'll fire off all the cannon in the navy. So go; retire to your chamber, and rely on me.—But stop—stop—as I can't get on quickly, owing to this infernal ballast
—do lighten me, will you? —do take part of a friend's load, Charles.

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: I thank you: but a stranger has forestalled your generosity.
— See—not an hour ago, I received this letter.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: From a stranger!

—“One, who pities the unfortunate,—who was the friend of Mrs. St. Orme, and suspects that the present baronet prosecutes you and secretes her, solely to keep possession of the large estate—sends you the enclosed, in the wish that it may lessen your afflictions, and assist in restoring you to her, whose best hope is in your affections.”—Upon my word, a charming correspondent!—can't you guess?

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: Oh, yes: her messenger betray'd her— her name's Honoria Pembroke.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Honoria! my Honoria!—don't fancy I'm in love with her, Charles—because, you see, I'm in love with somebody else;—but I tell you what—I wish you'd let me keep this letter—I should like to look at it now and then;—and if I thought nobody look'd at me, I should like—
Oh, bless her!
—and if she were present, and the whole world present, I'd serve her in the same manner. But adieu!—and with such friends fear not success.

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: And with such friends I've consolation if I fail; for the best passport to a happier world is approbation from such hearts as yours. Farewell!

sp.speaker: Henry
sp.p: Oh! who else can write such lovely, such bewitching—what other female hand can—Damme, there I go again—I forget her ladyship; and though she never honour'd me with any specimens of her penmanship, —further than merely writing “Pay the bearer” —yet with her elegant, accomplish'd mind— Oh! if she writes but as she talks—then is her style all tenderness—all—

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: Sir, your very humble servant. They told me you were here, and so I did come to ax your honour a bit of a question.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: What! a poor prisoner!—

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: No;—thank you kindly, sir—at present I do outdoor work with farmer Nightshade at Ivy-farm; and he did send me this morning to ax for a new serving lad; and so I did think the best place to hear of such a thing was the public-house—and who should I meet there, but Thomas!—your man Thomas:—and so over a mug of ale—he! he! —by gom!—if it's she, she's a lucky lass!

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Who?—who is lucky sir?

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: Why Bell—cousin Bell to be sure. We do think after getting her name chang'd to Miss This, and Mistress That, and Widow T'other, that at last she be come a real downright lady; my lady—oh ay—my Lady Sensible; and you see, I should like to know the truth of the matter: because if Bell a got this prefarment, it was'nt koind and pretty of her, to let poor I stay at plough—or her sister Sal cry matches and sell alincompain—or her brother Jack, for a slight pig affair, be sent out of this very place to Botany-bay.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Blockhead!—Lady Sensitive your— why, she'd faint at the idea!

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: Faint!

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Ay: 'twould so shock her sensibility—

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: Sensibili—what! she do sob and scream and laugh and tumble?—by gom! it's she! —Bell always had a deadly turn for fits and feeling and flourishing, owing to—
—that's the fact—I know it, you see, because since she left the farm I've been somewhat in the flourishing way myself; but whilst she staid, I had no chance of any sensibility at all.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Rascal!

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: Honoria!—nan!

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: On Lady Sensitive I mean—plague on't! —to be between wind and water, is one thing— between two fires, another—but between two women! —oh Belzebub himself could not be cool in the contest!

sp.speaker: Robert
sp.p: It's she!—cousin Bell's my lady!—and I—dang it—I wonder what I be; I suppose a sort of a man of honour at least—mayhap, a kind of a half lord; something like the mayor of our town here. But stop now, Bob—don't you be counting your eggs before you are sure the thing's sartin.—And where to learn this?—Oh—from his uncle—I'll go ask him directly; and if I find I'm really of this pretty koind of pedigree, and you come cuffing and collaring, Mister Sapling—I'd better take care though—what with practice and lessons, I dare say Bell has taught him to try my sensibility that way also.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE.—An Apartment in Delauny House.— In the Flat three Gothic Windows formed of Transparencies—the Centre Window exhibiting the Painting of the “Vestal buried alive,” very large and marking—the two other Windows of a less Size, with any fancied Transparencies.— Being Night, the Windows are not illuminated.— On one Side is a Picture not finished, with Apparatus for Painting; on the other a Table, with Books, Papers, and Candles upon it.—Sir Edward Delauny and Paul Postpone discovered sitting near it.

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Yes, sir! my conduct needs not vindication; I can avow it to the world.—On my accession to the title and estate, I found this wretch imprisoned for atrocious murder—his wife confin'd for lunacy incurable; and whilst respect for him I represent bids me seek vengeance on the vile assassin, humanity still prompts me to secrete the wretched, lost Amelia.—Am I not justified in both?

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Why, I don't like off-hand opinions, Sir Edward; my plan is to recur to law books:—but I rather fancy you've no power over the lunatic.

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: No!—Then read Sir Frederick's will—made on the morning of his death.

“I die in peace with my unhappy daughter, and in the case of her recovery bequeath her my estate for life;—but to preserve it from her husband's power, I nominate my nephew her trustee, and on her death devise the whole to him.”—Now, is she not at my disposal?—and if the villain should escape from justice, shall he e'er know the place of her confinement?—No— never.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Never!

sp.speaker: Sir. Edw.
sp.p: No—till they can prove she's restor'd to reason—and that's a hopeless prospect:— none dare arraign me!—But, to prevent his ever interfering, let us secure conviction; and this witness —on whose sole evidence his fate depends— this stage-struck daughter, who professionally knows all arts, all stratagems—oh! if she 'scape our search, is there no other way?

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: None! no witness—no verdict.

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Then let me haste again to seek her; and if found—of course you have prepar'd the necessary process.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: What pro—oh! aye:—the subpœna. No; I've been so taken up with other parts of the case—but I'll tell you what—I'll fill it up this moment
—this moment—
. Heh! where's that delightful music?

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: In the next room—and they'll disturb and interrupt you. I'll stop them as I pass.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Don't, on my account. I like music— often sing a merry song myself—and as there's nothing else, after filling up this little affair—'gad, I'll make one amongst them

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: You forget—the pleadings are not half prepar'd, and every moment of your time is precious
. Honoria! what brings you here?

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: I come by Mrs. Sapling's orders, to paint a copy of that representation of the “Vestal buried alive.”

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Well, well, dispatch—for it shall be remov'd—the sight is hateful to me.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Why hateful, sir?

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Why?—Oh nothing, nothing—but yonder's my solicitor; and mind that you disturb him not. And now, sir—be but as active and as zealous as the cause deserves, and our success is certain
sp.stage: (Exit. Honoria previously seats herself, and begins painting, unseen by Paul—he during the time is writing).

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: I'll be active—I'll—now that I call a complete idle country gentleman, who will let nobody have any pleasure but himself; however, only let me fill up this infernal process, and see if I a'n't in the thick of the musical party; for after such a fag as this, devil's in't if I mayn't enjoy myself; and music's a thing I'm doatingly fond of. So—“Herefordshire to wit”
. “Lovely, lovely Chloe!”

sp.speaker: Honoria
sp.p: Upon my word—extremely well—pray sing on, sir.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Sing on!

. Bless my soul—another thing I'm so doatingly fond of!—and look here now—I hav'n't even time to— oh, you little rogue!—I only wish it were the long vacation—but as it is—“Herefordshire to wit,”— “Lovely, lovely Chloe!”

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: That's right: you've an excellent voice, and I'd rather you'd do any thing than carry on this cruel prosecution
. Perhaps by some neglect of his, St. Orme might still be sav'd—I'll try—Oh! Lord, here's my guardian!

div.stage: Enter Sapling with manuscript music in his hand.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Oh, my dear Honoria!—what shall I do?—where shall I go?—whom shall I apply to? —Poor Mrs. Sapling—and poor Mr. Privilege!

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: What's the matter, sir?—any accident!

sp.speaker: Paul
sp.stage: (putting the subpœna in his pocket, and coming on the other side of Sapling).
sp.p: Aye! what's the matter, sir?—any accident?

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Dreadful!—he's taken hoarse! now—an hour before the sylvan fête, Mr. Privilege is taken hoarse, and there's an end of his and my wife's duet.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: An end of their duet!

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Yes: I offer'd to take his part here

: but it seems my voice is too natural. They say I'm no singer, because I don't quaver, and jerk, and twist my body, and make horribly ugly faces—and it's very wrong of them—I know it's all affectation—for I'm sure in their hearts, they'd rather hear such a queer fellow as I am, sing “Old Ramjudrah,” than all the fine flourishing songs in the universe.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: So they would—and at the end, applaud, as I applaud at the opera.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: What! do you applaud at the opera?

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Always—for joy that it's over.—But you want a substitute do you?

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: He does: and can't you recommend one, Mr. Postpone?

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: I!—Oh fie, ma'am!—I hope you don't insinuate—

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Speak to him guardian—his voice is only equal'd by his modesty.—Nay: you know it's true:—and by your own account, you've toil'd enough for this day.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: I have—I've work'd like a horse; and if I thought the ladies wish'd it—
sp.stage: (going to take the music from Sapling)
sp.p: —but no—Sir Edward will be angry.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Nonsense!—as master of the house 'twill be doing him a favour.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Will it?

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: To be sure—and you won't be out of the way you know.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: No more I shall!

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: And if you refuse, a great singer must be sent for at a great expence.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: So there must—and if I sing a hundred songs, I can but charge 6 s. and 8 d. each!—come along—give me the part—let somebody play it over —and once in my life, I will relax for half an hour.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: There's a noble lawyer for you!—Oh I wish I had known you sooner—you should have drawn my marriage settlement.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Never mind—where there's law and parchment before marriage, there's generally law and parchment after; and if any little accident should happen—
—between ourselves, now-a-days married people are the best clients.—But come;—and don't be afraid of my being natural—no—my voice is like an instrument.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Ah! that's the true style. But, begging your pardon, if it be the fashion for fine singers to resemble instruments, I wish there were instruments to resemble fine singers:—then they might be had at a less price—would be free from colds and hoarsenesses—and instead of Venice and Naples, they might be manufactur'd at Sheffield and Birmingham.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE.—A Road.—In the back Ground, large Gates opening to a Park—the Trees at a distance are seen illuminated—an Orchestra also—all marking a Sylvan Fête.—Stage partly darken'd.
Enter Sir Edward Delauny and Servant through the Gates.

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Discover'd, say you!—go on—repeat the joyful, welcome tidings.

sp.speaker: Servant.
sp.p: Yes sir; we saw her stealing out of yonder wood: and so whilst William staid to watch and to observe her, I came to ask your further orders.

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: And you are sure it is Lauretta St. Orme!

sp.speaker: Servant.
sp.p: Quite sir; we recollect her on the fatal morning—and see! she comes this way.

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Wish'd for, enchanting sight!—go— inform my solicitor—bid him come instantly, and bring the process that secures her—I'll stay myself, and guard her.

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Oh, thanks to that sheltering wood, that hitherto has thus preserv'd me; and if I reach again my lone retreat, none but a father's voice— ha!—What lights are those?—surely I hav'nt lost —oh yes—fear, and the darkness of the night, have quite misled me—Heavens!—let me fly—

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Stay—pass not I command you.

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Oh! for mercy!

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Mercy! from whom?—from him who represents Sir Frederick!
—Ay: behold your mortal, deadly foe; who long has sought, but now will never lose you.

sp.speaker: Lauretta
sp.p: You cannot— you will let me pass!—consider, by detaining me, you make me guilty of the very crime of which you charge my father.—He gave me life:—will you compel me to destroy his?

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Peace!—I'm resolv'd.

sp.speaker: Lauretta
sp.p: Look at me—'tis said I bear a strong resemblance to my mother— my poor ill-fated mother!—and shall my rashness rob her of a tender husband's care? Look—do I not remind you?

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: You do—and therefore is your presence still more hateful.—Yes:—she first debased our noble house's name, by marrying with this outcast.

sp.speaker: Lauretta
sp.p: She!—do you censure her!

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: I do;—and to complete the degradation, did she not abroad expose her daughter on a public stage?

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: How!

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Train her disgracefully in that low, mimic school—

sp.speaker: Lauretta
sp.p: No, sir—that fault was mine— I saw her perishing for want—my father helpless and infirm—and though, as a woman, most professions are denied me, the stage was still before me! —and I shall ever bless those kind approving hearts that sanction'd my attempts; nor call that path disgraceful, that leads a daughter to support her parents.

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Have a care—dare not to vindicate—

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Sir!—the stage requires not vindication —Is it a crime to labour to instruct and entertain?—Is there in Shakspeare's hallow'd lines, such ignorance and vice, that 'tis degrading to repeat them?—No, sir:—the day of prejudice is past —in public life, let there be private virtue, and the poor player will be more respected, than those who censure and despise her!

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: So she is—and every body should respect actors—because they always pay such handsome compliments to us British sailors.

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Heavens! Mr. Henry!

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Ay, sir—what brings you here?

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: I came to claim your promise, Sir Edward —as visitor at your house, by my uncle's introduction, you bade me ask for what I like—now I don't ask such serious favours of you, as shooting or fishing on the best part of the manor—because, I've heard, it only puts you country gentlemen to the trouble of whispering your game-keeper, to take one to your neighbour's grounds—no—in the way of sport, I simply beg leave to carry off this bird of passage!

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: 'Sdeath, sir!—I insist—

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: And I insist, sir!—I knew her in a country where there are some savages; but none bad enough to wish her to convict her father—or if there were, do you think I'd suffer it?—no—I'm afraid of only one human being, and as she's at an agreeable distance, I wish you good night, Sir Edward.

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Hold, sir—desist!—
sp.stage: (Noise of stamping with feet without, Sir Edward looks round.)
sp.p: Ha! I defy you now—for here comes one vested with legal power to secure her! Dare you contend against the law?

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: all the music of the spheres couldn't have cheer'd you—come, Lauretta—this is the first time I ever fled from an enemy; but if by my retreating you escape, 'twill be the proudest victory I ever gain'd!

div.stage: Enter immediately from the Park Gate Paul Postpone, the MS. Music in his Hand.

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Now, sir—are you completely ready?

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Quite, sir—“To arms, to arms”—
Oh, I beg pardon, I thought it was Mr.—but I perceive now; you want the subpœna—here it is— all prepar'd you see.

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: I do—and look, yonder goes Lauretta —follow her—make sure of her; and, lest her champion should molest you, and my appearance may be thought vindictive, I'll seek and send assistance. Away—lose not a moment—my happiness, my reputation—nay, my life depends on your success.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: I'll do it. I'll serve the process in spite of her and all her champions.—
sp.stage: (As he is going a flourish of grand martial music is heard.)
sp.p: —Bless my soul! it's beginning! the music is beginning! and now at the moment, when I should have cut such a figure!—Was there ever such an infernal laborious profession?

—Yes: there they are all seated—all the sweet beautiful ladies, waiting to applaud my vocal and instrumental powers— dear! dear! Wouldn't it be time enough to serve the subpœna early to-morrow morning? I've often put it off till the last moment; and no man living has ever lost—I mean, gain'd, more causes than I have done.—But then, Sir Edward and his reputation!—Oh—I must go after her.

div.stage: Enter Sapling through the Park Gates, hastily.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Oh, Lord! I'm so glad I've found you. Come along—
The sweet creatures are all on the tip-toe of expectation.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: I know it. So am I—but look, look at that tormenting witness.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Witness!—Where?—I see nobody.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Don't you!—faith!—no more do I.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: No: whoever they are, they're safely out of sight for this night.—So—nonsense! stuff! put it off till day-light; and now it's the assizes, recollect you've a right to enjoy yourself!—Isn't it a part of the business to have balls—concerts—

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: So it is; and if barristers partake of them, why not attornies?—damme, I won't be the slave I have been!—I'll let my genius take its bent; and if it ordains me musical, it's a better trade than mine—more profit—less trouble—

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Ay: and as a reward for your labours, applause and repetition; but in law!—now I only ask, Who ever claps a declaration?

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: No: or who ever encores a bill in Chancery? —come along.—“To arms! to arms! we heroes cry.—Huzza! to victory!”
sp.stage: [Exeunt singing to grand martial music, which continues after the dropping of the curtain.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Positively, Honoria, I will not listen to you. You really must marry Mr. Privilege —and soon—very soon!—for my own wedding is gone by, and I begin to want something new dreadfully.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Nay, madam: when I've told you that from early life, my heart has been another's—

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Simple thing!—she don't know that hearts have been out, ever since pin-money and separate establishments came in. And surely you don't compare the elegant Mr. Privilege with this barbarous sailor gentleman?—In the first place, the man has no voice.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: No, ma'am: no more has Mr. Sapling.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: No voice!—my husband!— Oh, I understand—you mean that I play the first instrument?—Vastly well!—and so you shall find, ma'am—though a widow—though not quite so young and striking as Miss Honoria—there is now-a-days this consolation—old women never go by—and whilst my voice lasts, neither his nor yours shall be heard, I promise you.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: No, madam: and till my guardian shall assert his rights, I have no hope of happiness or Henry.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: None—if 'twere only for his insolent insinuations.—Brute!—monster!—to speak such home truths—to say I dreaded seeing my husband on horseback, because his fortune was in annuity, when every body knows my love for poor little Sappy is so violent—so—

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: I say the fault's yours—and so I'll tell my client again and again.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Then I say you are a base slanderous person.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Mercy!—What's the matter, gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: The matter, ma'am!—Why the assizes have began; and owing to this seducing deceiver, our only witness has escap'd.—You know it, sir. You bade me put it off till day-light; and now, for the first time, I shall be set down as an idle, dissipated—

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: And so you ought—for the music didn't content you—no—you must dance also—and play billiards also—and bet against time also.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Don't you talk of betting against time? Didn't you offer to trot on your own feet against post horses; and draw chaises with your own hands against dray horses?—In fact, didn't you so completely prove yourself a four-legg'd animal, that at supper, when you ask'd for ham and fowl, the company beg'd you'd stand on no ceremony, but call for hay and corn as if you were alone?

sp.speaker: Servant.
sp.p: Sir, we have trac'd young Mr. Sapling and the lady—they took the road towards Ivy Farm—and Miss Lauretta is disguis'd in boy's clothes.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Disguis'd in boy's clothes!

sp.speaker: Servant.
sp.p: Yes, sir—in a green coat—white waistcoat —round hat—

sp.speaker: Paul
sp.p: Enough; that, with her effeminate appearance, is full description.—Shew the way, and, free from dissipated company, I'll secure her.—

—Madam, yours.—If at any time you want legal redress—and with such a fashionable husband, the thing's not at all unlikely—there's my card: neat house—and charming accommodation for you and the female part of the family;—but for the male—extremely sorry, but there's no stable on the premises.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Stable! Make me out a four leg'd animal! —Excuse me, my dear—but nobody shall take such liberties with me but yourself. Besides, to suppose I'd even name a horse, when—

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Oh, the odious creatures!—for Heaven's sake, don't let them make me a disconsolate widow a second time, Mr. Sapling.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: They sha'n't. You sha'n't be a widow, my darling—and what's more, Honoria shall be a wife—she shall marry Privilege directly; and as for Mr. Henry—leave him to me—I've laid a train that will blow him out of water.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: A train!

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Mum! He keeps a lady.—Robert Grange, a Yorkshireman, informs me he keeps a cousin of his in London; so what do you think I've done?—sent Robert off express; bid him tell his cousin of Henry's love affair with Honoria—and then you know, down comes her ladyship—she gives it him one way—Honoria another—Robert another—

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling
sp.p: So they do.—Poor wretch!—What will become of him?

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Aye: he may stand against the cannon's roar;—but two jealous women, back'd by a Yorkshireman—damme, the rock of Gibraltar could not resist their artillery.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Oh delightful!—Mr. Privilege is now in the park; and I'll immediately inform him.—But though this is very well for such women as Honoria and her self-created ladyship; it won't do in fashionable life—you'll never find me jealous, Mr. Sapling.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: No—nor me, my dear. When I hint that you sometimes speak and look too kindly on your admirers—it isn't jealousy!—no—it's pity —general pity for mankind.—I wish you to be merciful, and spare those murdering smiles—

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Do you?—Well! Perhaps I will be merciful—adieu!—You really improve every hour, Mr. Sapling.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: I do!—I'm finish'd!—it's very odd, though—if I weren't convinc'd that jealousy was out of fashion, I should be sometimes like Othello —quite black in the face with it!—for here's Mr. Privilege—how can I tell but she may go on pitying him, till every body pities me. Very well! —I know how to be even with her—I can go hunting and break my neck at any time.

sp.speaker: Groom.
sp.p: Sir!—Sir!—Your favourite hunter—

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Hush!—lower—or your mistress may hear you.

sp.speaker: Groom.
sp.p: Sir, your poor mare Arabella, is so low spirited for want of hunting, that I do think the next time I take her to the river, she'll coolly lay down, and drown herself.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Poor Arabella!—she's a charming goer; and if your mistress would give me an opportunity, William—but no—she's so loving—so dutiful—so constant—

sp.speaker: Groom.
sp.p: Ah!—it's a thousand pities, sir—but perhaps mistress mayn't be always so, sir.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: No!—Why not, sir?—Have you heard any thing?

sp.speaker: Groom.
sp.p: Not at present, sir—but I hope for the best.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: You do; do you?—Leave the room. —No—stop—follow me to the library, and I'll give you a prescription for the mare:—and as to your wishing your master to be a—; no, sir, I am sufficiently fashionable without that embellishment.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE.—A lone Farm-House, with much marked Desolation around it.
Enter Hnery Sapling and Lauretta St. Orme. Lauretta is disguised in Boy's Cloaths.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Come, come, cheer up.—Look—yonder's Ivy Farm—the lone sequester'd house we are in search of;—and thus disguis'd, and introduc'd as servant to the farmer—

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Aye: but the time—the time!— think in a few short hours, my father will be summon'd to the awful scene, and if he blesses not the daughter who preserves him, he'll curse the parricide whose rashness has destroy'd him.—Oh! I can't bear the recollection. Hide me from heaven, the world, and from myself.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: No—I'll only hide you from your enemies. —Hush—stand aside—somebody approaches.

div.stage: Enter from the House Sternly and Farmer Nightshade.

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Enough—I'll tell Sir Edward.—Good day!

sp.speaker: Nightshade.
sp.p: Good day!

sp.speaker: Sternly.
sp.p: Remember now—be more than ever wary.

sp.speaker: Nightshade.
sp.p: Fear not—this secures me
: but plague on't; I can't manage without a servant; and this Yorkshire rascal that I sent for one—what the devil is become of him?

sp.speaker: Henry
sp.p: It's he!—I know him now
. —So, Master Nightshade, you want a servant, don't you?

sp.speaker: Nightshade.
sp.p: I do, Squire Sapling—want one mainly—and sent my ploughman—

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: I know it—and I've brought one—see
—I'm sure you'll take my recommendation.

sp.speaker: Nightshade.
sp.p: That I will, sir—and thank you for this timely service;—besides, I like the lad's countenance—he looks discreet and trusty:—come along, boy.—Only this, sir—I hope he don't mind solitude—we see nobody at Ivy Farm.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: All the better—is'nt it, boy?—there —now you're safe, till I inform your father, and return
.—Adieu!—You've got a treasure, Nightshade.

sp.speaker: Nightshade.
sp.p: I think I have, sir—and as to my lazy Yorkshireman—if he don't come home directly, he shan't come home at all.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: And serve him right

. —Low-lifed, scurrilous blockhead! —I dare say he is now all the time at the public-house, boasting that he's cousin to a lady.— Well—with all my heart—I only know it is impossible he can be a cousin to my lady.—Yes:— there's a native elegance—a sort of noble indescribable —and I'd a dream that so reviv'd and rivetted my love—

—Heh! who is walking yonder with that coxcomical—By heaven! Honoria, and the husband they design her!—and see —he kneels to her—he kisses her hand—and she permits it!—So, so—she likes him—she prefers him!—Oh! after all, give me the woman who turns off cooks and lap-dogs; not her who selects privileg'd men—and that decides it.—I'm for her ladyship and London.

sp.speaker: Thomas.
sp.p: Sir, Lady Sensitive has sent me posthaste with this letter.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: I'm glad on't. I long to hear from her —I sigh to see her dear delicious hand!—Oh, that —that for the false Honoria's letter
sp.stage: (taking it from his pocket, and throwing it down)
sp.p: . —Now let me dwell on a superior composition—
. “You know too well my tender nature; and if you do not set off for London directly, you will never see me more.”—Sweet innocent! how I have neglected her!—

“Never, you saltwater savage!—Thanks to your uncle, Bob is arriv'd—my Yorkshire cousin Bob, sir!—and if you don't quit this Miss Honoria Thingambob, I'll come down—shoot you—stab her— and poison myself!—My head goes round and round—I write this between my fits—and have already emptied the laudanum, hartshorn, and all the other bottles in the house.—Your's, &c. A. Sensitive.”—Pheugh!
—I shall have a fit myself—Thomas! you don't believe that is her ladyship's hand, do you, Thomas?

sp.speaker: Thomas.
sp.p: Sir, I saw her write it.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Did you, Thomas?—Perhaps then I didn't read it rightly—I'll just look again—
sp.stage: (Takes up Honoria's letter by mistake, and reads)
sp.p: . —“One who pities the unfortunate—who was the friend of Mrs. St. Orme,”—Confusion, shame—
.—Oh fool! fool!—And you, sir—you, who must have known this gross deception—

sp.speaker: Thomas.
sp.p: Nay, sir—what could I do?—nothing would open your eyes—nothing!—for don't you remember, in one of her faintings, when you sent for the great physician?

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: I do—and 'stead of physic, he prescrib'd bank notes;—and on putting a twenty pound one into her hand, she leer'd at it, jump'd up—and went shopping directly!—Oh, I perceive it now— brought up at sea and in the country, I know but little of the world, and never shall—seeing no joy in guilt myself, I can't conceive how others should pursue it.

sp.speaker: Thomas.
sp.p: Aye: but how will you stop her, sir? she'll come down and kill us all, and—Oh Lord;—here she is—I'm frighten'd out of my senses.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Frighten'd!—at what, blockhead?
—Look out—does she seem very violent?

sp.speaker: Thomas.
sp.p: No, sir—Now I look again, it seems a different person.

sp.speaker: Henry
sp.p: Yes: it is a different person —Honoria flying from her lover! treating him with scorn and indignation!—and look here now— I'm more afraid of her than of the other;—I can't encounter her kind virtuous smiles, because I feel I don't deserve them—I'm all perplexity and fear —pick up the letter—come along this moment; and if you'd never be the wretch that I am, take a wife, Thomas—Oh, there's rapture in the word— a wife to me is a ship well man'd, a prosperous pilot, a successful voyage, victory, prize money, and first lord of the admiralty.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Gone! avoid me!—leave me to the mercy of this insulting coxcomb!—Surely it was Henry: but perhaps he saw me not; or if he did, knew not the serious danger I'm exposed to.— Alone, unprotected, and menac'd by an artful wretch, whose heart's unmanly as his form; who, with a look effeminate, conceals a savage and ferocious mind. How shall I shun him?—how reach home in safety?

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Very well, that's Ivy Farm; and Lauretta is disguis'd in a green coat, white waistcoat, round hat—enough. Tell Sir Edward that the witness is secure, and, in law or in music, that Paul is first fiddle.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Oh, Mr. Postpone, I'm so glad to see you. Now I'm safe—I'm sure you'll give protection to a timid, helpless woman.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: That I will—but as I told you before, it must be in the long vacation—I hav'n't a moment now—unless, indeed—Lord! she's quite overcoming—and, if I thought witness wouldn't escape again—but no, no—away, Cupid!—Remember it's the assizes.—

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Then I must protect myself—for yonder's my tormentor, still seeking to insult me—Sir, I shall not reproach you, but when expos'd to insolence and peril—

sp.speaker: Paul
sp.p: Oho! —are you there, my little—“toll de roll loll.” —

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: How! treat me with ridicule and scorn?—Oh Henry! is it not hard that none have feeling to defend and save me?

sp.speaker: Paul
sp.stage: (still looking out and recurring to his pocket book).
sp.p: Green coat! white waistcoat! round hat!— “toll de roll loll.”

div.stage: (N. B. Previously to this Scene, he must appear in Green Coat, &c. so as to resemble Lauretta's Dress as nearly as possible.)

sp.speaker: Privilege.
sp.p: There she goes. Oh Lord! how I am fatigu'd!—But I'll after her!

sp.speaker: Paul
sp.stage: (coming before him, smiling, and putting his hat before his face with one hand, and with the other offering the subpœna).
sp.p: Take it, will you?— I'm naturally so modest and—. Really the very thought makes me blush so, that upon my soul I'm asham'd to look at you. Take it, will you?

sp.speaker: Privilege.
sp.p: Asham'd to look at me? Why who the devil are you? and what's this?

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: The subpœna, you cunning little rogue! and the next time you disguise yourself, do it better —for to pay you the compliment that's due to you, so far from any thing coarse or masculine, curse me if ever I saw a more feminine delicate creature in my life; never;—and I shan't want gallantry —no, as you are fatigu'd, you shall have a horse; and hark'ye, a nice soft side saddle!

sp.speaker: Privilege
Paul.
sp.p: Man! that's a good joke; as if nature ever meant such a thing as that, for one of my noble gender?—And as to her strutting and blustering; does she think I don't know one sex from another? Pooh; go where she will, I'll go after her; and bring her before the Court, if it's only for a libel on the nation; for if it consisted of no better men than she is, we should be all Bond-street beaus, men-milliners, butterflies, and jackadandies.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE—Inside of the Farm House, Stairs leading to a large dark-colour'd Door, a great Iron Chain across it, Chairs, Table with a Jug upon it.
Enter Nightshade and Lauretta St. Orme.

sp.speaker: Nightshade.
sp.p: Aye aye, if you like retirement, this is the house for you. In the first place, you are never to stir out; and when I do, you are to expect to be lock'd in.

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Lock'd in, sir!

sp.speaker: Nightshade.
sp.p: Ay: and you are not to write letters or receive any; and on no account to admit visitors.

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: No, sir!

sp.speaker: Nightshade.
sp.p: No—you are to see nobody, but myself, a nurse, and another person: look at that door, that with the chain across it.

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: I see, sir; you terrify me beyond description: let me go.

sp.speaker: Nightshade.
sp.p: Nonsense!—'tisn't to imprison you; no, 'tis secur'd in that manner for secret purposes; and, when assistance is requir'd, you must be ready to afford it. And now, I've told you your employment, do as your predecessor us'd to do— come,
, enliven me with a song.

sp.speaker: Lauretta
sp.stage: (looking at the door with great agitation).
sp.p: Sir, I—I—

sp.speaker: Nightshade.
sp.p: Nay, I am master here, and will not be refus'd—sing, I insist; it will amuse us all.
Lauretta!

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Ha! that voice!
Help! help, Lauretta!

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: My mother, it is my mother's voice!
sp.stage: (running towards door and beginning to unbar it).

sp.speaker: Nightshade
sp.p: Hold—Who bid you unbar the door?

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Instinct, which impels the offspring to assist its parent!
sp.stage: (Lauretta throws back the chain, door opens and discovers a dreary apartment, lamp hanging in it; Mrs. St. Orme falls in Lauretta's arms.)

sp.speaker: Nightshade
sp.p: Stir not, she's my prisoner.

sp.speaker: Henry
sp.p: And you're mine.—If taknig prisoners be the plan, a British sailor 'gainst the world, my boy.

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme.
sp.p: Lauretta! though thus disguis'd, I trace each well-known feature;—and that bounteous power that long since bless'd me with returning health, restor'd my harass'd and disorder'd mind, now makes me feel the blessing ten times o'er; for I behold and know my child again. Oh! I'm most grateful!—but that stranger—is he not a foe?

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Heaven forbid, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: No, he's the best of friends, and will conduct you to my father.

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme.
sp.p: Your father!—Never, never!

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Never!

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme.
sp.p: No, his falsehood first derang'd me; and that he since has doom'd me to captivity, I have unanswerable proof—His letter; oh, his letter written to the late Sir Frederick, and shewn me by Sir Edward's agent.—

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: His letter!

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme.
sp.p: Ay, his!—I knew the once lov'd hand too well, and the indelible and cruel words can never be effac'd. “I charge you to confine her; if she escape, my misery is everlasting.” —Oh! this from him! from him, the father of Lauretta!

sp.speaker: Henry Sapling.
sp.p: Madam, my life on't, he is wrong'd.

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme.
sp.p: No, sir; this, with his falsehood, is sufficient proof; and I retort the accusation of derangement—the road to happiness is virtue; those who forsake it are the truly mad, and if this treatment of a doating wife be not insanity, 'tis worse, 'tis vice, and I would rather pity than despise him.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: I say again, he's wrong'd; but this is not a place for explanation; let me conduct you to some safer spot.—And for you, Mr. Solitude— you see that spare room? say two words and I'll shut you there, with no food but your reflections; no company but your conscience: they were this suffering lady's best support—but if you were a navy, they'd sink you, hypocrite!

div.stage: Enter Thomas, in great haste and agitation.

sp.speaker: Thomas.
sp.p: Sir! sir!

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Come! arriv'd!

sp.speaker: Thomas.
sp.p: Yes, sir—

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: At the door! in the low chariot with her Yorkshire cousin! and to catch me with two such lovely—Oh, this will never do, I'll sneak and hide myself

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: How! Do you hesitate? Will you at last forsake us?—Look! look on my mother.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: I do—and it's coming—I'm screwing myself up, I'm comparing my own paltry danger with such distress as hers, and—your hand, ma'am, I'm ready for action!—But, at the same time, there can be no harm in your sticking close, Thomas.

sp.speaker: Nightshade.
sp.p: Hold, sir—none stir without my leave.

sp.speaker: Henry
sp.p: Your leave!—that's a good joke—when I've made up my mind to engage a seventy-four, do you think I'm afraid of a common cock-boat? —go—go before I insist, sir; and tell the enemy, if they dare fight against two vessels shipwreck'd and distress'd, they must be cowards; and, spite of cousins, cuffs, cordials and faintings, I'll convey both to harbour!—I, Henry, the friend of them, of marriage, of Honoria!

div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE.—An Apartment in Delauny House—a Door in the Flat leading to a Bed-Chamber.

sp.speaker: Privilege.
sp.p: So: I've got clear of him—I've at last escap'd him and his side-saddles, and subpœnas, and I begin to suspect his business now.— It's a writ—he has got a writ against me from some curst taylor or other; and if I'm arrested at this moment, I lose Honoria and her thirty thousand pounds; but she's safe now; I'm sure to catch her, before he catches me.—No—damme! here's the horrid brute again!—Where shall I go?

This door's lock'd!—and yonder's Mrs. Sapling's bed-chamber—she's not in it though; or if she were, my character would there bring me off; but with lawyers and bailiffs— somehow I never could convince them I'm a privileg'd man.

div.stage: Enter Paul Postpone time enough to see him.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: I see you my darling! I see you; and should have come up with you sooner; only I stop'd to look at a cricket match.—He! he! it's pretty sport;
and I should have won more on the runs, than these two guineas, only the dull dogs left off play to go to business.— But now for it—
sp.stage: (goes to the chamber door and tries to open it.)
sp.p: —Foolish little thing! as if that would save her.—Holloa! there's the subpœna under the door—that's a good service—and thus the iron hand of law—

But stop; now in Sir Edward's house, and guarded by his servants, she may be safer here than under my protection—she will! so I'll step over to the townhall, see how cause stands; and then return, and whisk her like a whirlwind to the trial: and after this, let no man charge me with the law's delay. Never was such diligence and zeal.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Come along; I know you meant to elope. I know the letter was from Henry, and when Mrs. Sapling has nam'd a husband for you, how dare you love another man?

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Nay, sir—because she controls your feelings, is she to command mine?

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: She is; and I'll call her from her bed-chamber —and if you don't instantly marry Mr. Privilege—

sp.speaker: Paul
sp.p: Oh fie! fie! force her to marry one man, when you know she loves another—not that I allude to myself—no— whether I am or am not the happy object of her choice, this she may depend on; I'll release her in the long vacation:—and for you Mr. Sapling; don't trust yourself near that chamber; nor on any account peep through the keyhole; for fashionable as you are, you'll blush—But I can't stay to explain particulars: must step over to the town-hall— so, mum—Don't you go near that chamber.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Not go near my wife's chamber!—not peep through—Oh Lord! surely—pooh, nonsense; she only treats poor Privilege as a plaything: and whilst other ladies make pets of cats, puppies, and monkies on four legs, she chuses one on two legs, that's all.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: And you'd have me marry a monkey, sir?

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Why not? Put a monkey on a short coat, long pantaloons, thick neckcloth, cropt wig, large opera hat, and there's as good a husband as the best of them;—and you shall have him—and spite of that fellow's scurrilous insinuations, I'll venture to call Mrs. Sapling—yes—I'll—
hold, as usual, let me announce my approach by an elegant tap—

sp.speaker: Privilege
sp.p: Is it you, Mrs. Sapling?

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Privilege
sp.p: Is it you, my dear Mrs. Sapling? or is it that horrid brute?

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: It's he!—he calls me horrid brute! There's the privileg'd man—and here's the finish'd man!—Within there! William! William!

sp.speaker: Honoria
sp.p: What's the matter, sir? What are you doing?

sp.speaker: Sapling
sp.p: When I lov'd and doubted, I was miserable; now I know I'm a horrid brute, I'm completely comfortable.—
Come William, come and saddle Arabella —to horse! to hunting! to the field, my boy!

sp.speaker: Groom.
sp.p: What! Have you got leave, sir?

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: No: I've taken leave.—She has her favourites—I'll have mine;—come, and saddle Arabella; and if being jealous is being ill-bred, so much the better; I hate fashion; I like feeling; she has cut me to the heart, William—now I'll break her's, and we'll be both buried in the same grave!

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: What can this sudden alteration mean? No matter, it gives me momentary safety; and I may once more read my Henry's letter.

“I have so offended Sir Edward, that I dare not venture to his house; but as I hope you take an interest in my fate, I write to tell you, I am at the Star, a small inn on the skirts of the town, where I am detain'd on secret and important business.—For Heaven sake, if your enemies continue their persecutions, remember you may command the friendship, heart, and life of your adorer,Henry.”Oh! the wish'd for hour is come—at last I know I am belov'd by Henry—and could I 'scape this hated roof—
sp.stage: (Here Privilege opens the chamber door and peeps out)
sp.p: then might the husband of my heart be mine; not him whom cruel force decrees me.

sp.speaker: Privilege
sp.p: Very likely; but you shan't escape ma'am—no—

here I am, red hot with wrongs and disappointments—and dread my mighty and resistless anger. Yes: though in form diminutive; in soul, Goliah was a dwarf to me! Answer me; Is he not a sailor, and would you prefer pitch and tar, to the essence of taste and politeness?

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Sir, I prefer feeling to foppery; manliness to effeminacy; and a poor sailor, with nothing but his fame to recommend him, to one who thus displays the valour that he boasts of— not in the service of his country; no, in insulting unprotected women.

sp.speaker: Privilege.
sp.p: And you'd be rash enough to leave the house!

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: I would; the rashness is in staying here—here, where each moment teems with danger. —Let me pass—let me seek him who is alone my friend, and whom I'll follow through the world.

sp.speaker: Privilege
sp.p: Hold! recollect where you are—in mine and Mrs. Sapling's power; and till our marriage, this room shall be your prison!—Ay: I'll fight him and his whole ship's company, sooner than—

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Come along—trial's on—court waiting— witness call'd for—nay: no delaying—this way you little rogue! this way.
sp.stage: (Takes him in his arms, and carries him off.)

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Alone! in safety!—now then for love and Henry!

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: She is secur'd you say!

sp.speaker: Servant.
sp.p: Yes, sir; and Mr. Postpone bade me inform you, he was so sure of success, that, no doubt, by this time, the prisoner is convicted.

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Then I am safe. It never can be proved, he died a natural death—
Go, watch the trial, and when his doom is certain, be swift as lightning to inform me.

— Oh yes: Lauretta's evidence is final, for he who proffer'd medical advice, and knew the wound ne'er caused Sir Frederick's death, is purposely abroad.—I live again—my character is unimpeach'd —St. Orme will never meddle or torment me, and his Amelia and her proud estate are still at my disposal.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: So Sir Edward—Have you heard?—

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: I have. I've heard that you secur'd Lauretta, and that secures my triumph.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: No; it don't: for owing to my extreme zeal and activity, instead of a lady in boy's clothes, it turns out, I subpœna'd a little man! and so, for want of evidence, the prisoner is acquitted.

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Acquitted!

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Ay; to the joy and satisfaction of the whole court: for they whisper'd strange stories of Sir Frederick dying a natural death; and when they told them to me, says I: “I'm sorry then I took such uncommon pains, and if Sir Edward is not of my humane disposition, I should regret doing him an injury, but I'd never—never try another cause for him.”

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Fool! blunderer! you know not half the danger I'm involv'd in; you've set a lion loose to menace and pursue me.—What's to be done? rescu'd himself, he will release his wife!—I must prevent it—instantly prevent it; and for you— whose folly and delay has ruin'd—has destroy'd me—

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Delay!—it's no fault of mine. When I was told the lady's dress, was I to stare, and pry, and examine?—and if I had, unless this Mr. Privilege would write the word “man” on his forehead, the devil himself wouldn't know him to be one.

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Sir, you've undone me; and that others may not suffer by such wilful ignorance, and gross neglect, I will expose your errors to the world. Nay, sir; if I'm disgrac'd, you shall not pass uncensur'd.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Expose my errors! try to knock me up in my profession! when every body knows I've been hurried out of my senses; and that business can't be well done, unless a man has time to do it coolly.—However, I must look about me; I must still give up enjoying myself, and get another lawsuit, if it's only to convince him and the whole county, that with a good client, clear case, and strong evidence, no man has more success than Paul—

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: Sir, your humble servant—I hope I don't mistake; but if you be the wonderful London lawyer they do talk of, I've a bit of a job for you.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: You have, have you?—talk of the Devil —I'm he! I'm the wonderful London lawyer!

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: By gom! I thought so; and I like your looks at first sight; you seem to have so little pride—so little of the gentleman about you, sir.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Thank you—and I'm happy to be able to return the compliment; but your case; state, state—

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: Why, you see, sir, I be not a person of rank myself; but cousin Bell be my lady, though I be none; and poor soul! she a been cast away like a weed by a base deceiver—and when he came out of Ivy farm, I'd certainly have stopt him, and got an understanding; only Bell fitted it beyond her usual mark, and claw'd me so tight by the throat, that he got off; and here I am, as you see, sir, without any understanding at all.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Enough—see your case at one view— plaintiff, unsuspicious country girl; defendant, rich seducer; domestic peace, parental love, filial affection, paradise, Eve, Satan, dark night, rope ladder, post-chaise and four, and a thousand pounds damages—only wish she were a married woman, and you her husband—that's the valuable action; but as it is—What's her name?

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: Why she do call herself Lady Sensitive; but I suppose that won't do with you lawyer gentlemen; and so, between ourselves, her real name is Bell—Arabella Grange.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Arabella!—very well—and her seducer's?

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: Sapling; and you'll find him yonder, at the Star inn.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Sapling! Oh ho—thought so—thought this would come of the old fellow's fashionable habits— know him well; and see, if I mistake now—see, if this case don't confirm my reputation; and difficult as it is, I'll get you an understanding
. But stop—let it be moderate—don't expect a great one.

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: No: our terms are quite moderate; Bell only requires that he'd settle on her all his own fortune, and all this Miss Honoria Thingambob's; and as to myself, I shall be satisfied if he'll just promote me to the rank of major or colonel— either in the army or navy, I don't care which, sir.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Don't you?—it's done then.—An hour hence meet me at the Star inn; and bring your cousin with you; and we'll have a bit of dinner; always mix pleasure with business, one helps the other; and only be ready with your evidence— no disguises though—no getting into petticoats— no—come forward as witness—and I'm a wonderful lawyer.—Arabella, a rich lady; and you, a major or a colonel, in the army or the navy!

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: Dang it—as I said, not a bit of the gentleman about him; but somehow, I'm sorry he do want me as witness; I can't bear the thought of these examinations and cross examinations, ever since they brow beat me so at last 'sizes:—“So,” says Counsellor Bounce, “your name is Robert Grange, is it? Well! and pray what is your opinion of this case, Master Robert?”—“Why, I take it,” says I, “you are paid for your opinion Master Counsel, and therefore I'll thank you for a fee, before I give mine.”—“Silence!” says he, “and upon your oath, are you not such a notorious poacher, that you are commonly call'd snaring, thieving Bob?”—“Yes, I am,” says I, “by such low chaps as you are; but never by gentlemen; and if you'll step out, and have a snug, friendly round or two, why I'll wager this half guinea”— and then I felt for my purse and couldn't find it; and so I fell a blubbering, and charg'd them all with picking my pocket, and then they laugh'd, and turn'd me out of court!—but I'll to Bell; and if this master lawyer do provide for us, why I'll be so grateful to the whole tribe, that I'll give them my opinion gratis, whenever they ask for it.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE.—The Outside of the Star Inn.—In the Back Ground an open Country.—Trees at the Wings.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
