sp.p: Don't you be afraid, William. I'll keep my ground; I'll vex her in my turn. I'll join the hunt, dine with the club, sing, game, and destroy my own health in toasting other people's; and if I drink myself dead, I know she won't survive me: and if I get dead drunk, why, then I'm a philosopher—above her, and the miseries of this life.

sp.speaker: Groom.
sp.p: Ay, sir, this is all very well now; but suppose mistress were present.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Then I'd avow it to her face. Go, prepare my favourite, whilst I dress in the inn. Oh yes, the chace inspires me! and dogs and horses shall afford that solid joy, that love and wives and monkies would deny me. I'm up!— the lion's rous'd!—an earthquake wou'dn't shake me!

div.stage: Enter Honoria, with her Hat and Cloak on.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Heavens! how my heart beats! Yonder is the inn; and yet I fear that Henry will condemn me. Perhaps he knows not my immediate danger; but, surely, when he hears it, he'll
—Ha! all hope is past; I am pursued, discovered.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Vastly well!—as I was informed. Caught you in the fact of eloping, on the very eve of setting out for Scotland! But come, madam; and if you persist in the excursion, let Mr. Privilege conduct you.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Never! Coward as I am, I will not give my hand but where my heart's dispos'd of: and Henry, generous Henry, is its owner!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: What! Mr. Sapling hasn't told you then? You hav'n't heard of this rival?

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Rival!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Oh yes; there's a mistress in the case. The generous, artless Henry keeps a creature—

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: I'll not believe it; the heart that's capable of virtuous love must scorn all baser passion; and here
he tells me he's devoted to Honoria. Look!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling
sp.p: I do; and it seems, “he's in that inn, and detained there on secret business.” Oh, why secret? My life on't, because the lady is now with him. I know Mr. Sapling sent for her, and therefore—Landland! landlord!

sp.speaker: Landlord.
sp.p: Madam!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Tell me, sir, isn't there a naval officer, a Mr. Henry Sapling, in your house?

sp.speaker: Landlord.
sp.p: There is, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: And is he alone? That is, isn't there a lady with him?

sp.speaker: Landlord.
sp.p: Yes, ma'am, there is a lady with him.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: There! Now are you satisfied?

sp.speaker: Honoria
sp.p: One moment. Perhaps it is Lauretta? Pray, sir, is the lady very young? About fifteen, sir?

sp.speaker: Landlord.
sp.p: No, ma'am: she seems to be nearly thirty; but very handsome.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: And you are sure, quite sure, that it is Henry Sapling?

sp.speaker: Landlord.
sp.p: Quite, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Come, madam, I'll go home, and do whatever you require of me, and cheerfully; for I'm happy, quite happy
; and I'll never think of the false, false Henry more.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Won't you? Poor girl!
Oh barbarous, inconstant man?

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Inconstant man? and in tears! you've heard then?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: We have, sir: his falsehood is detected.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: I thought so. When I gave you my card, I fear'd you'd find him out; but there's this consolation—your damages will be greater than Arabella's.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: My damages!

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Aye; you are an amiable, deserted wife; but Arabella—

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: I a deserted wife! Peace, sir! and know 'tis Henry Sapling—'tis his nephew that—

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: His nephew! Pooh! that's very well to blind you; but that sort of cover won't do for me. No; and since my reputation rests upon this case, and I'm tir'd of being libell'd for other people's blunders, I'll have him out, and prove—

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Do, sir: convince yourself, and this distrustful girl, that Henry is this Arabella's swain, and that my doating husband, who never wanders from my apron strings, and who is now at home waiting with anxious—
sp.stage: Enter Sapling, from the Inn, strutting, and in a hunting Dress.
sp.p: Mercy on me! here, in the inn! Speak, sir—how came you—
sp.stage: (Sapling passes by her, and goes towards the wing.)
sp.p: Why, what are you doing?

sp.speaker: Sapling
sp.stage: (pretending not to see or hear her).
sp.p: William! Is my favourite ready?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: What favourite? Heavens! Surely you don't mean this creature, this Arabella?

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: I do mean Arabella; and I avow it— boast of it. I have secretly concealed her a long time; but now she shall have more of my company. I'll go out with her every morning, visit her every evening, keep her an additional servant, have drawings, paintings, statues made of her— in short, curse me if I don't think I'll live with her.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Astonishing! live with her!

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Why not? She will be careful of my neck, though she has no annuity upon it! And you, Honoria, you shall also share my favour; and we'll return to the farm, and never more quit it for faithless, fickle, cru—
. There! I've shewn my spirit. And now, come along, girl.

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Thank Fortune! Henry's affection is confirmed.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Thank Fortune! my reputation is confirmed. And that Sir Edward may know of my success—come, madam; I'll attend you to Delauny House!—And, for this little gay deceiver, depend on't, we'll bring him on his knees.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Ay: he shall sue in vain for pardon; and, for the rest—oh! I wish, with all my heart, my first husband were alive.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: So do I, with all my soul; then you'd have finished him, instead of me.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: Enter Henry, Mrs. St. Orme, and Lauretta.
N. B. Lauretta is in her own Cloaths.

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme,
sp.p: May Heaven unite you to Honoria—hearts such as yours can best reward each other—but, to my purpose; that you, my child, no more may suffer by the frowns of fortune, first let me claim my lost hereditary rights, and then to seek abroad that happiness denied me here.

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Abroad!—You cannot; you will see my father.

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme.
sp.p: No, he has deceiv'd me once, and may again confine me. Like you, I triumph in his late success, and wish my charges were as groundless as Sir Edward's—but no, his letter is decisive! and therefore come to Delauny House, and there we part, my child.

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Part, mother!—Speak, intercede for me, sir.

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme.
sp.p: Yes; part, Lauretta! I to some foreign clime, and you where duty and affection dictate—he has no crimes to you, and though I thus could cling for ever round you, I will not rob him of a treasure he deserves. No, he has accustom'd me to sorrow, and I can proudly wish him happy, happy with his daughter.

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Why, why won't you speak, sir?

sp.speaker: Henry Sapling.
sp.p: I do, ma'am—don't you see I'm speaking all the time? not with my tongue, that sticks to my mouth; but my eyes, my hands, my heart, are all speaking; and when a sailor's on shore, I don't think it kind of his friends to be always soaking him in this manner with salt water.—
—Besides, there's danger at Delauny House.

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme.
sp.p: What danger, sir? the estate is mine; I go to claim it for my child; and in such a cause, fear can't assail me.—Come, and when you've found your friend, speak not of me; or, if you do, I will be silent and avoid him.—Oh yes; to him I'm still a coward; but to Sir Edward and his haughty friends, I'm firm as pride, maternal love, and conscious worth can make me.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Indeed!—I wish she'd spare me a little of her firmness; for between her, and St. Orme, and Honoria, and another lady, I'm fairly flurried out of my senses.—Gad! I don't know which I think most of.—Yes I do, though; her ladyship's is the lasting impression! I shall never forget her! and as a proof she won't forget me, look, here's her curst Yorkshire champion.—Zounds! once in these scrapes, a man never gets out of them.

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: Sir, your very humble servant—I— I—Oh Lord! what will become of me?

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Peace, sir; none of your sham sensibility—

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: Nay; it's all downright earnest now: for you mun know, I went to a lawyer about your casting off Bell; and when I got back to the tavern, I found she had cast me off!—Yes, you see she had a knack of never fainting properly, unless there was somebody to look on; and so she got blubbering at the window, and one Captain O'Sash saw her, and nodded, and—dear! dear! I can't contain myself.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: No more can I!—Go on, melodious messenger—proceed, seraphic orator!

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: One Captain O'Sash, I say, nodded and tript up stairs; and soon after, Bell order'd the low chariot, and away they both went to a French foreign place call'd Tipperary—yes, Tipperary— and further, I'm sorry I can't tell you.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: And so am I; for I could dwell for ever on that silver sweet ton'd voice—and for this friendly captain—Oh! blessings on him! I'll go see Honoria directly.

sp.speaker: Robert.
sp.p: Od dang it! what, won't thee try to bring her back again?

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: No, curse me if I do—and that you may not attempt so rash an act, here's money to drink them a pleasant journey.

And now for that delicious darling hope, a wife, fire-side, children, pure domestic love. Oh, generous, noble captain!May all his future days be gay and airy In the sweet bowers of love and Tipperary.

sp.speaker: Thomas.
sp.p: Sir, I ax pardon; but, to avoid detection, and get time for escaping, I understand Farmer Nightshade has given out that Mrs. St. Orme is dead.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Dead!

sp.speaker: Thomas.
sp.p: Yes, sir; and Sir Edward believes the report.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Indeed! let the plot thicken, then. Tell St. Orme, he'll find Lauretta at Delauny House.
And may he there again partake connubial joys.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Connubial joys! That's right, Henry. Come and enjoy them. Come, and marry Honoria directly.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: What! consent! let me have a wife at last!

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Ay; being in for't myself, the more the merrier, I say.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: So say I. Oh! if every body knew the blessings of matrimony as much as I do, England would treble its inhabitants; and its most valuable property would be old bachelors and old maids; for they'd be taken alive, and shewn as curiosities.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE.—The Library, with Painting Apparatus and transparent windows, as in 2d Scene of the 2d Act—only, being day-light, the Windows are now illuminated. —Lauretta is discover'd painting Letters on the Vestal buried alive—at the Top she has already written the words “Edward Delauny,” and at the bottom nearly finish'd those of “Amelia St. Orme.”—Mrs. St. Orme is discover'd with her.

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme.
sp.p: Desist—desist, Lauretta!—this libel on Sir Edward will never vindicate your father.

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Nay, dearest Madam, I have nearly finish'd; another letter will complete the work. There!

.—Thus let the mystery be solv'd, be this the touchstone of Sir Edward's conduct! And if it prove as I suspect, that he's the real culprit, think of the bright reward—you, mother! you still shall bless Lauretta and her father.

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme.
sp.p: Oh! if I thought there were a hope! but no, 'tis past; and therefore to avow my claim—

sp.speaker: St. Orme
sp.p: Where is she? Where is my daughter?

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme.
sp.p: Heavens! So near me! my shatter'd brain can't struggle with the conflict!—

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Stay, I implore you, stay.

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme.
sp.p: I cannot! dare not! no, within this room I may remain conceal'd; and, since I gain'd admission here unnotic'd, unobserv'd, none can betray me but yourself.

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Fear not, for I bless the lucky chance, that thus enables you to hear and judge how you have wrong'd my father.

div.stage: [Mrs. St. Orme exit at stage door.
Enter St. Orme and Sir Edward Delauny.

sp.speaker: St. Orme,
sp.p: Think not I came to menace or intrude; no, sir, I came on Henry's suggestion, to seek my dear lov'd daughter; and what strange motive brought her to this place, she shall explain hereafter. We owe no favour to Delauny House, and never will!
sp.stage: (Crosses to Lauretta, takes her hand, embraces her, &c.)

sp.speaker: Sir Edward
sp.p: And I myself should scrutinize her motive, but that Amelia's death makes me defy all fear—Oh yes, the dreaded tale died with her; and therefore
, take a last farewell of this proud house, that still so galls and irritates —
sp.stage: (Crossing, he sees the transparency, and starts)
sp.p: . —Ha; whose deed is this?—“Edward Delauny!”

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Ay; and “Amelia St. Orme.”— What alarms you? Why should a picture agitate you thus?—I tremble not; no, nor my father!— See, though the story shocks his tender nature, he turns not from it with remorse;—No, the faithful husband and the ardent lover break forth in mingl'd tears of pity and affection!—
.— Oh Heaven!—I said—I knew that he was innocent!

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: Explain, Lauretta. What means that—

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: Means!—That that lovely suppliant is my mother: and that the hand that robs her thus of liberty and life, is her exalted kinsman's, who treats the stage with scorn and indignation, when but a mimic scene like this can goad the guilty, and reward the good.—Father! you must, you shall be happy!

sp.speaker: Sir Edward.
sp.p: Audacious girl! who dare accuse me of such crimes?

sp.speaker: Lauretta.
sp.p: I, in the face of Heaven and of man —I will aver, that to retain this splendid edifice and proud domain, you thus immured the best of mothers and of wives—if not, behold the picture firmly, like my father.—See! he dare not—Oh, guilty!—on my soul he's guilty!

sp.speaker: Sir Edward.
sp.p: 'Tis false—and were your mother here, she would accuse another.

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: What other, sir?

sp.speaker: Sir Edward.
sp.p: You know too well. Nay, dare not to deny it—here's damning proof against you.
—“I charge you to confine her—if she escape”—

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: Oh villain!—curst contriving villain! —if that which tenderness and pity prompted, has been perverted to such savage purpose, may every husband's, every father's curse—But no, guilt such as this, is so unparallel'd, that we should pray for mercy, not for vengeance.

sp.speaker: Sir Edward.
sp.p: Away, and know she died the victim of her malady.

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: Died!

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: Ay: and by her decease, I sway for ever here:—and mark me, sir; if rashly you revive the charge, this letter shall acquit me to the world.—No other witness can be found—

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme.
sp.p: There can—and I'm that witness! —My life! my husband! after such proofs, shall I delay to clasp you to my heart?—No: the story of your falsehood was contriv'd like this, from treacherous, sordid motives; and henceforth my suspicion is reserved for those who would destroy domestic peace—my love and confidence for him and her, who know no wish beyond it!

sp.speaker: St. Orme.
sp.p: Share—share my joys Lauretta; alone I can't support them.—And you, Sir Edward—

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme.
sp.p: Upbraid him not: his triumph was to punish, ours is to pardon.—Yes, sir—
the virtuous best resent their wrongs, by deigning to forgive them.

sp.speaker: Sir Edw.
sp.p: I see I am betray'd, and need not your reproaches; my own, and that reproachful look are quite sufficient; and thus disgrac'd, I shall renounce all future claim; for fortune, rank, and life, are equally indifferent!—farewell!
and to relieve you from those bitter pangs that goad and torture here, know, 'twas the hand of Heaven, not your's, that doom'd Sir Frederick to his grave.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: What! going, cousin! now, when I expect the bride and bridegroom!
—and leave your company!—You're vastly welcome though
sp.stage: (curtseying to St. Orme, Mrs. St. Orme, and Lauretta)
sp.p: ; and I expect my penitent husband, and with him, Honoria married to Mr. Privilege: these are the terms of my forgiveness, and so Mr. Postpone is gone to inform him.
Here they come. I ordered one of my grand marches to announce their arrival.

div.stage: Flourish of Music, and enter Sapling, Henry, Honoria, and Paul Postpone.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Oh joy! my dear Mr. Privilege! a thousand joys!

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: You're too good—and in return, allow me to introduce to you Mrs. Henry Sapling!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: What!

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Mrs. Henry Sapling; and to save you the trouble of telling her of my past follies, I've told her myself, and she generously forgave me; and for any further information on this subject, I refer you to Captain O'Sash at Tipperary; and for any information relative to the bridegroom you expected, I refer you to the taylor who has just arrested him; so there end his privileges—and here begin mine

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Why, Mr. Postpone, hav'n't you explained?

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: He has; he told me how Privilege got into the bed-chamber, and I told him that my Arabella was related to Hambletonian, Rockingham, Ticklepilcher, and Potatoes; but, as usual, he came too late. He stopt to follow the fox chace. So, by his delay, I've lost a dear good wife, and Henry's gain'd one.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Don't blame me; I told you all along there was no doing business by driving and hurrying. —And twenty attornies wou'dn't be sufficient for such a fashionable family as you are. But, I give you joy, ma'am

; and if I've time, and your husband's leave, I'll visit you every long vacation.—And I give you joy Mr. St. Orme; and should they traduce me for not convicting an innocent person, should they say I'm not a sharp and active lawyer, so much the better—I know I'm an honest one, and I'll delay to alter that character as long as I live.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Come, since we are all united—since, as I hoped, Henry and Lauretta have regain'd their prize—shall nunky have no wife?—Come, madam, come—

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: Mrs. Sapling! my life! my—that's a good sign—silence is a proof of love.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Indeed! then I fancy few married ladies are in love—but I'm too well bred to wrangle; so, there!

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: And there!

sp.speaker: Henry
sp.p: And now henceforward copy me uncle; —think not of any Arabellas: or if you do—be it to pity those, who, but for men's seducing arts, had known, like us, the bliss of virtuous love!

sp.speaker: Honoria.
sp.p: Then crown our pleasures with your genial praise, Blame not our Blunders, pardon our Delays. All aid my suit.

sp.speaker: Henry.
sp.p: Let me your favour court; A married sailor begs you won't spoil sport.

sp.speaker: Sapling.
sp.p: So does a fox-hunter
a finish'd man.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Sapling.
sp.p: Ay, ladies, look—refuse him if you can.

sp.speaker: Mrs. St. Orme.
sp.p: And we entreat you—

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Yes, and Paul Postpone. Your smiles are fees for all his labours done. Each cheering nod demonstrates he has great sense, And every clap's a glorious six and eight pence, Then, take the hint, and, spite of critic laws, We'll to an English Jury trust our cause.
